name: Coda alla Vaccinara (Roman Braised Oxtail)
why: The quintessential Roman winter braise - oxtail melting away in tomato, celery and white wine, finished with a secret twist of dark chocolate that deepens the sauce without a trace of sweetness. Peak November cooking: browning, then hours of hands-off low heat.
author: Henry
ingredients: 80g lard, cubed (or a knob of beef dripping)
2 celery stalks, cut into pieces (added later)
2 garlic cloves, peeled and roughly chopped
1 tsp unsweetened cocoa powder (or 20g dark chocolate)
salt and black pepper, to taste

steps: Dice the onion, carrot and one celery stalk finely - this is the soffritto.
Set aside the other two celery stalks; they go in at the 2-hour mark.
Heat the olive oil in a large, deep heavy-bottomed pan over high heat.
Add the oxtail and brown well on all sides - you want a real crust, not just colour.
Remove the oxtail to a plate and set aside.
In the same pan, saute the diced onion, carrot and celery over low heat in the remaining oil until soft.
Add the lard, parsley and garlic, and cook a few minutes until the flavours have melded.
Return the oxtail to the pan and cook a few minutes, then pour in the white wine.
Let the alcohol evaporate completely, then add the passata. Season with salt and pepper.
Cover and braise over very low heat for at least 4 hours.
Check every 30 minutes: stir occasionally, make sure the meat is not sticking, and add a splash of hot water or stock if the sauce looks dry.
After about 2 hours, add the two reserved celery stalks.
Once the oxtail is falling off the bone, add the cocoa powder (or dark chocolate).
Stir until melted and cook 2-3 more minutes, then turn off the heat. Serve with bread or creamy mashed potatoes to soak up the sauce.

pro_tips: The chocolate is the Roman secret - it rounds out the tomato acid and gives the sauce a glossy, deep, almost meaty richness. Start with the cocoa; add a little more if you want it stronger.
Oxtail needs a low, lazy heat - the moment it starts bubbling vigorously, it will toughen and the sauce will emulsify wrong. Patience is the whole technique here.
